newsitem.title: UK: British court delays Spanish fish case to 1997.
newsitem.headline: British court delays Spanish fish case to 1997.

text.p: Spanish fishermen claiming millions of pounds in compensation for being banned from fishing in British waters were told on Tuesday they would have to wait almost a year for their case to be heard.
Britain has vowed to fight the claim, which a government minister said showed a "crazy situation" has developed as a result of the European Union's fisheries policy.

David Vaughan, lawyer for the Spaniards, told a preliminary court hearing that the owners of 97 fishing vessels had probably lost a million pounds ($1.55 million) each when they were prevented from fishing between April 1989 and November 1990.
Judges in the English High Court decided on Tuesday to hold a pre-trial review of the case in February next year followed by a full hearing in June or July.
The European Court ruled in March that British laws which restricted foreign-owned fishing vessels from operating in British waters breached European law.
But Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry told BBC radio there was no case for the Spaniards to be paid damages.
He said Britain was seeking far-reaching changes to the European Union treaty to end "quota hopping" which enables foreign vessels to register in Britain and take part of the national quota catch.

"What this does demonstrate is the crazy situation that has arisen in relation to quota hoppers, whereby, in effect, Spanish owned, crewed and skippered boats can come and fish as against the U.K. national fishing quota," Baldry said.
"We cannot have a situation whereby U.K. fish are being taken by anyone other than U.K. fishermen. That's just crazy and the sooner the quota hoppers are eliminated the better," he said.
The activities of the Spanish trawlers have infuriated British fishermen, who have been forced to cut back on their catches because of European Union conservation policies.

Jim Portus, spokesman for the South West Fish Producers Organisation, said fishermen in his area had been losing about 25 million pounds ($39 million) worth of fish a year since the decison by the European Court.

But Anton Gonzalez, manager of a Spanish company which operates four boats out of the Welsh port of Milford Haven, said he believed he was as entitled to fish British waters as the operator of any other British-based craft.
"We have been fishing here for the last 15 years and we feel that we are perfectly entitled to part of the quota. We have the same rights as any British vessels," he told reporters.
